extracted.intended_audience: novelists, serious students of fiction, and literary critics
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on choosing narrative method and dramatizing consciousness in novels — when to use first-person, third-person, epistolary forms, and how to 'show' a mind rather than merely report it. Emphasizes economy, indirect (dramatic) methods, and techniques for making thought visible.

rubrics_metrics.name: First-person as pictorial/intervening narrator
rubrics_metrics.description: The first-person narrator is valuable where the novelist must rely on an intervening storyteller to present a pictorial vision — 'it is much more satisfactory to know who the story-teller is, and to see him as a part of the story.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use first-person to lend dramatic energy to pictorial scenes and to make clear who transmits the view (examples: Dickens, Thackeray). It enhances verisimilitude when a seeing agent is needed to select, interpret, and compose the scene.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations of first-person when narrator is the subject
rubrics_metrics.description: When the main weight of the story lies in the narrator's own life or inner change, the first-person report becomes overtaxed and inadequate — 'the method has a certain dramatic energy... but for a subject like Meredith's it is really too little.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid relying on retrospective first-person narration to render a searching, elaborate portrait of the narrator's consciousness; such a narrator can only 'report' and cannot convincingly dramatize the inner life. Consider shifting method if the narrator must be himself vividly present to the reader.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dramatize a mind rather than accept its self-report
rubrics_metrics.description: The novelist should, where possible, make a character's consciousness visible and active in the text rather than merely allowing the character to describe it — 'the novelist... represents [the mind] by means of the movement that flickers over the surface of his mind.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show impulses, reactions, and the evolution of thought as if they were actions on stage (Henry James's technique). This produces a stronger, more immediate conviction than a character's retrospective account (examples: Strether, Raskolnikov).

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorial withdrawal to let the character's thought tell the story
rubrics_metrics.description: The author should often stand aside so that the story is told through the character's thought-world rather than by the author or by an interpreting narrator — 'the author does not tell the story of Strether's mind; he makes it tell itself, he dramatizes it.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Techniques include rendering the mind's processes directly in the narrative (free indirect style, interior focalization), so the reader watches the mind 'in action' and gains access to the character's evolving perception without explicit authorial commentary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer indirect (dramatic) methods when possible
rubrics_metrics.description: An indirect, more circuitous method of presentation often produces a straighter, more effective result for the reader — 'the more circuitous procedure on the part of the author produces a straighter effect for the reader.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim to place the thing itself in view (people and action appearing independently) rather than relying on explanation. Progress the telling toward drama as far as the subject allows.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economy: do not over-treat the subject
rubrics_metrics.description: Push the method only so far as the subject profits; over-dramatization or unnecessary exposure of a mind can displace the story's centre and harm the work — 'the method is to be pushed as far as the subject can profit by it, but no further.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide by the nature of the subject whether increased dramatization adds value. Example: David Copperfield needed no higher dramatic value; over-enriching the hero's inner life would have displaced the true subject.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use epistolary/diary form to capture contemporaneous emotion
rubrics_metrics.description: Letters or diaries can dramatize a mind's agitation by making emotion contemporaneous — 'Reading her letters, you hear the cry that was wrung from her at the moment... the spectacle of her bearing under such terrible trials is immediate and urgent.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose epistolary form when the subject is the unfolding of feeling or comportment under strain. Be aware of drawbacks: contrivances to preserve verisimilitude, implausible logistics, and potential limitations in scope (Clarissa and Grandison examples).

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not let the narrator stand between reader and active mind
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid placing the hero or heroine as an obtrusive mediator between reader and their emotions or thought when living drama is possible — 'do not let the hero come between us and his active mind.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the central interest is the mind's activity, prefer methods that present the mind directly (dramatization, interior focalization) rather than allowing the character to filter and report their own inner life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Select point of view according to the subject's requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: The best method of telling is guided by the subject itself: whether to let the story speak for itself and to conserve economy. 'The point is indicated by the subject of the story itself.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the subject needs independent appearance of people and action or whether it needs the reader to share a particular vision. Let this twofold consideration (desire for drama + economy) determine the narrative form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make the reader share the character's vision while keeping access to the mind
rubrics_metrics.description: Render the scene through the character's perceptions but also present the character's internal energy so the reader can follow the mental process — 'The scene... is watched through his eyes; but now there is this other fact... his consciousness... is before us.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance external pictorial description with dramatized presentation of interior life. Techniques: focalization that allows the reader both to see what the character sees and to witness how the character's mind converts impressions into meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Embodied signs of thought: let looks, behaviour, and surface movement reveal inner life
rubrics_metrics.description: Like a play where a character must reveal thought through words and deeds, the novelist should use the 'look and behaviour of thought' as the vehicle by which story is rendered — 'The impulses and reactions of his mood are the players upon the new scene.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Translate mental states into observable actions, gestures, tones, and minute perceptions in the narrative so the reader can infer the inner process without explicit exposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware the costs of contrivances that preserve a narrative device
rubrics_metrics.description: Methods that serve to dramatize (e.g., keeping characters at a distance so one can write letters) carry costs that can strain verisimilitude and narrative practicality — 'The visible effort of keeping all Clarissa's friends at a distance... seems always on the point of bearing him down.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When adopting a device (epistolary, strict first-person, etc.), weigh the dramatic benefit against narrative contortions required to sustain it; avoid devices that end up handicapping the story's plausibility or scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: The novelist can dramatize without sacrificing panoramic vision
rubrics_metrics.description: Making a mind visible does not necessarily forfeit the novelist's freedom to take broad views — a dramatized mind can still 'lend us eyes' and provide panoramic suggestion via concise means.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use dramatization (showing inner life) alongside the novelist's ability to compress time and summarize scenes (a word, a look, minutes for months) to retain scope while achieving immediacy.
